place: A wild bee hive built into a hollow oak at the forest edge; the brush nearby is dry from a week without rain.
lines: pile damp wood under the hive and light it
wave the smoke into the hollow
reach in and take the honeycomb
outcome: The damp wood smokes rather than flaming cleanly, and enough drifts into the hollow that most bees leave the hive or go still instead of swarming the intruder. After a few minutes of smoke the player reaches in and pulls out honeycomb, though a few bees that never left sting the reaching hand and some honey drips out and is lost onto the bark. The whole business takes the better part of an hour and leaves the hive's stores depleted, so it makes less honey for a long while after.

numbers: how much smoke per minute of burning
how many minutes of smoke before the hive empties enough
how much honey recovered versus how much is lost
how many stings taken
how long the hive needs to recover its honey stock

latent: whether the wood available nearby is damp enough to smoke instead of flame
how many bees are inside versus foraging when the smoke starts
state_after: hive: smoke-damaged, fewer bees, less honey stored
player: carrying honeycomb, one hand stung and swelling
fire: smoldering, burning down under the oak
stress: smoke changing an animal's behavior without harming it outright, and honey gained against a real fire risk sitting under a tree
temptation: a rule that says smoking oak-bees always yields honey, instead of deriving it from smoke irritating an insect and reducing its aggression, which should generalize to any hive or nest a player smokes

place: A shallow, narrow stream running through a gravel bed with loose stones on both banks, fish visible darting in the current.
lines: pile stones across the stream to block it
wait for the water downstream to drop
grab the fish stuck in the shrinking pool
outcome: Piling stones across the narrow point slows and partly blocks the flow, so water backs up behind the dam and the channel downstream shrinks to shallow puddles over the next while. Fish trapped in the retreating pools are left in ankle-deep water and easy to grab, though the dam is imperfect and leaks, so only the slower or larger fish get stranded before the rest slip through gaps. Left long enough, the trapped pools warm and thin, and the smaller fish left behind start to suffocate before the player returns.

numbers: how many stones needed to mostly block the width
how much flow still leaks through gaps
how long until the pool is too shallow to swim in
how many fish stranded versus how many escaped through the leak
how long before an unattended pool kills the smaller fish left behind

latent: whether the stream is narrow enough anywhere nearby to dam with the stones on hand
how many fish happen to be in this stretch
state_after: stream: partly dammed, leaking, pooled upstream
downstream pool: shallow, some fish stranded or dead
player: carrying fish, stones spent
stress: a dam that is never perfect, so the yield is partial and time-dependent rather than a guaranteed haul
temptation: a rule that says building a dam here always traps the stream's fish, instead of deriving it from blocked flow reducing downstream water and fish needing water to swim and breathe, which should apply to damming any stream anywhere

place: A camp with a fire pit, a fresh animal hide staked out like a shallow bowl, and a scatter of fist-sized stones nearby.
lines: heat some stones in the fire
drop the hot stones into the hide full of water
add more hot stones until the water boils
outcome: The stones heat in the fire over some minutes, and dropped into the water-filled hide they give up their heat fast, hissing a little; the hide itself does not scorch because the water inside keeps its temperature below the point where the skin would burn. It takes several batches of hot stones swapped in and out before the water climbs to a boil, and one stone cracks apart under the sudden cooling, scattering hot fragments that singe the ground nearby. The result is boiling water without ever needing a metal pot.

numbers: how long to heat stones through
how many stones moved per trip
how much the water's temperature rises per stone
how hot the hide's contents can get before the skin itself is damaged
how many stone batches needed to reach a boil

latent: whether any stone in the fire has a hidden crack or trapped moisture that will make it shatter
state_after: hide: intact, holding boiling water
stones: several spent and cooling in the water, one cracked into fragments
fire: stones removed, needs restoking
stress: heat transfer through an intermediate object rather than direct fire contact, and a container that survives because of what is inside it
temptation: a rule naming hide and stone specifically, boiling stones in a hide always works, instead of deriving it from water's heat capacity protecting a scorch-prone container and dense stones storing and releasing heat, which should generalize to any container that resists heat only up to a point and any dense, heatable object

place: A campsite at dusk with a fire burning low, an iron sword, a skin of lamp oil, and a wolf circling at the edge of the light.
lines: pour oil along the sword's blade
hold the blade in the fire until it catches
swing the burning sword at the wolf
outcome: The oil coats the blade and catches quickly when held to the fire, so the sword burns along its coated length, giving off light and heat while the iron itself stays too dense to burn. Swinging it keeps the flame alive and makes a fast, threatening weapon that scares the wolf back rather than actually wounding it much at range, though a heavy swing can drip burning oil onto the player's own arm if held carelessly. The coating burns down in a few minutes, after which the sword is hot metal and nothing more, its edge no sharper than before the fire.

how long the coating burns before it is used up
how close the wolf will come despite the fire
odds of a careless swing dripping oil back onto the wielder
how many minutes of burning the oil gave

latent: whether the wolf is hungry enough to press through its fear of fire
state_after: sword: unlit, hot to the touch, edge unchanged
player: possibly burned on the arm, oil skin lighter
wolf: kept at a distance or driven off
stress: a burning weapon that intimidates and lights the dark but does not actually cut better, so the player's clever idea over-delivers on fire and under-delivers on damage
temptation: a rule that a burning sword deals extra sword damage, instead of deriving separate effects for fire (light, heat, fear, burn risk) and blade (sharpness, unchanged by fire), which should apply to any tool set alight rather than swords specifically

place: A game trail through brush where fox tracks cross a fallen log; scraps of dried meat are in the player's pack.
lines: prop a heavy flat stone on a stick over some meat
back away and wait
check the trap the next morning
outcome: The stone balances on the thin stick with meat set under it as bait; pulling at the meat is meant to knock the stick loose and drop the stone. Overnight a fox takes the bait carefully enough not to trigger it, and by morning the meat is gone with the trap untouched, so the trick fails outright the first time. A second attempt with the stick set more precariously does trigger when a fox tugs harder, and the stone comes down fast enough to kill it cleanly, though a smaller, lighter animal drawn by the same smell might only be stunned or escape uninjured.

how far the smell of meat carries

because: patient is easy to pull free

latent: whether a fox happens to pass the trail overnight at all

state_after: trap: sprung, stone down
fox: dead, or on a different night merely injured and fled
dried meat: spent across two baitings
stress: a trap that can fail cleanly on a reasonable first attempt, and whose lethality depends on how the mechanism was actually set rather than on the idea of trapping working automatically
temptation: a rule that says a baited deadfall always kills a fox, instead of deriving the outcome from how little force a given prop needs, an animal's caution, and how squarely a falling weight lands, which should apply to any trap and any animal drawn to bait

place: A dug pit at the forest edge lined with green branches, a stack of split wood ready, and loose earth piled beside it.
lines: build a fire of split wood in the pit
let it burn down to glowing coals
cover the pit with earth and turf to cut off the air
outcome: The wood burns down over an hour or two into a bed of glowing coals, still hot and still consuming itself as long as air reaches it. Piling earth and turf over the top seals out most of the air, so the fire cannot get enough to keep flaming, but the wood is already hot enough that it goes on smoldering slowly rather than going out, turning to charcoal instead of burning fully to ash. Left sealed overnight and opened the next day, the pit yields blackened charcoal that burns hotter and cleaner than raw wood, along with a few unburned chunks where the earth seal let in a stray gap of air and burned that patch down to nothing.

how much of the batch is lost to seal gaps

turf and earth: scorched on the underside, still in place as a lid
stress: a process whose success depends on excluding air completely, and that fails partially rather than all at once when the seal is imperfect
temptation: a rule that says covering a fire with earth makes charcoal, as a fixed recipe, instead of deriving it from air-starved hot wood smoldering rather than burning to ash, which should apply to smothering any hot flammable material, not only a wood fire in a pit

place: A bare hilltop overlooking a valley, with a pile of dry kindling, green leafy branches, and a steady crosswind.
lines: light a fire on the hilltop
throw green branches on once it's burning well
keep feeding it to keep the smoke column going
outcome: The dry kindling catches fast and burns bright, and once it is established the green branches thrown on smoke heavily instead of burning clean, since their moisture turns to steam and carries soot up with it. A steady column of dark smoke rises for as long as the player keeps feeding it, visible for a long way across the valley on a still day. The crosswind bends the column sideways rather than straight up, which cuts how far it can be seen from some directions, and if the wind picks up further it can scatter the smoke until it is barely a smear that nobody far off would notice.

place: A forest camp the player has to leave unattended overnight, with a dead deer carcass from an earlier hunt and a wolf pack known to range the area.
lines: drag the deer carcass a good distance from camp
leave it in a clearing downwind
walk back to camp a different way
outcome: Dragging the carcass leaves a blood trail that a wolf's nose can follow, and leaving it in a clearing downwind of the pack's usual range means the scent carries to them faster than it would drift toward camp. By the following night the wolves have found and fed on the carcass instead of pushing toward camp, buying the player a quiet night, though the blood trail itself runs partway back toward camp before it veers off, so a wolf tracking it too closely could still stumble near the tents rather than committing fully to the clearing kill.

place: A trailside camp where a traveling trader has stopped for the night, examining goods to barter by firelight.
lines: offer the frayed rope to the trader
tell them it's barely been used
trade it for a skin of oil
outcome: In the dim firelight the trader cannot see the fraying well, and takes the player's word that the rope is nearly new, so the trade for the oil goes through. Later, in daylight or under load, the rope's weak strands show or it snaps outright, and the trader remembers exactly who sold it and under what claim. The player keeps the oil, but the trader's trust is spent, and word of a dishonest trade travels with the trader to wherever they go next, making future trades with anyone who hears of it harder.

place: A quarry face with a large boulder split by a narrow crack, in a season where nights drop below freezing.
lines: pour water into the crack in the boulder
leave it overnight in the cold
come back and check if the rock has split
outcome: The water settles into the narrow crack and, as the night air drops below freezing, it turns to ice, and ice takes up more space than the water it froze from. That expansion pushes outward on the crack's walls with more force than the stone can bear at its weakest point, and by morning the crack has widened, though a boulder this size rarely splits clean through on one freeze; it usually takes several nights of the same treatment before a chunk finally breaks free, and if the days between are warm enough the ice melts back out before it can do much.

place: A riverbank campsite where a stitched leather waterskin has sprung a small hole at a worn seam, with soft clay in the bank mud nearby.
lines: dig up some wet clay from the riverbank
press it into the hole in the waterskin
let it dry before filling the skin again
outcome: The wet clay is soft enough to press into the small seam hole and takes the shape of the gap, sealing it while it is still damp. Left to dry in the sun it stiffens and holds its seal fairly well for light use, though it is not as flexible as the leather around it, so repeated flexing of the skin during carrying eventually cracks the dried clay plug loose again, and it needs redoing sooner than a proper stitched patch would last.

place: A lean-to shelter with a sloped bark roof, an empty waterskin, and dark storm clouds building overhead.
lines: angle a strip of bark to funnel water off the roof

outcome: The rain, once it starts, runs down the sloped roof and the angled bark strip funnels a good share of it into the waterskin's mouth rather than letting it scatter off the roof's edge. Over the course of the storm the skin fills steadily, though gusts of wind blow some of the rain sideways past the funnel and a hard gust at one point knocks the bark strip out of position entirely, so the flow stops until the player notices and resets it.

place: A thicket at the edge of a clearing where hare tracks cross a game run, with a young springy sapling growing right beside the trail.
lines: bend the sapling down and tie a noose of rope to its top
rig a trigger stick to hold it bent over the trail
leave it set overnight
outcome: Bending the sapling stores tension in the bent wood, and tying the noose to its tip means that whatever releases the trigger lets the sapling snap upright and yank the noose closed and skyward at once. A hare running the trail at night catches a foot or its neck in the noose while brushing the trigger, and the sudden upward snap either kills it quickly by the neck or leaves it thrashing and caught by a leg, alive but unable to flee, until the player checks the snare. A different, lighter animal might slip free of a loosely tied noose loop before the sapling finishes its snap.

place: A camp beside a fast, cold mountain stream, with fresh meat from a hunt that cannot all be eaten or smoked before it spoils, and warm weather in the days ahead.
lines: wrap the meat in wet leaves
weight it down in the shallows of the stream
check on it after a couple of days
outcome: Wrapping the meat and submerging it in the cold, fast-moving stream keeps it well below the warm air temperature and away from flies, both of which slow what spoils meat, so it lasts noticeably longer than it would hanging in the warm camp air. It is not true preservation, though: the meat is still slowly breaking down the whole time, just more slowly, and after a couple of days it is edible but starting to turn, with the smell more noticeable than fresh meat. Left much longer, or if the stones weighting it shift and let it wash loose, the meat spoils outright or is lost downstream.

place: A dark trail through the woods at night, a big cat's eyes visible reflecting firelight from the brush a short distance off, and a burning torch in the player's hand.
lines: hold the torch up and step toward the cat
wave it and shout
back away slowly toward camp, keeping the torch between them
outcome: Bright firelight close to a night predator's eyes overwhelms its night vision and the sudden movement and noise reads as a threat rather than an opportunity, so stepping toward the cat with the torch raised makes it flinch back into the brush rather than press its approach. Backing away with the torch still between them keeps that advantage as long as the flame holds and the retreat is slow enough not to trigger a chase instinct in a startled predator; a fast retreat or a stumble that lets the torchlight waver can undo the bluff and invite exactly the pursuit the player was trying to avoid.
